Discord re-introduces age verification policy based on 'account signal' methodology
Discord says it has built an age estimation model based on 'account signals' to determine an user's age group.
Diego Argüello
,
Contributing Editor, News
,
GameDeveloper.com
September 23, 2026
schedule
3 Min Read
Image via Discord
Discord is re-introducing its age verification policy eight months after its first attempt, saying it has built an age estimation model based on "account signals." Moreover, it will now be offering more verification options rather than exclusively asking users to submit face scans or identity documents.
In an
announcement shared yesterday
, penned by Discord CTO and co-founder Stanislav Vishnevskiy, the company outlined "more transparent" steps when it comes to age verification. This the second attempt after Discord said it
failed at its "most basic job"
with the initial February rollout, acknowledging that it knew it would prove to be controversial, and that it failed to clearly explain why it was being implemented in the first place.
The unclear communication led a large part of its user base to believe that almost everybody needed to submit identity documents or face scans in order to continue using the app. Vishnevskiy claims the contrary, saying that more than 90 percent of existing users won't have to go through age verification.

This is in part due to an age estimation model based on account-level signals (how long an account has existed) and payment methods on file, which are used to estimate a user's age and place them in either the adult or teen age group, the latter spanning the age of 13-17 and having additional protections.
If an user's account needs verification, Discord will now offer additional verification methods than don't require an ID or video selfie. These include credit cards, Apple App Store, Google Play Store, Google Waller, and AgeKey. Some methods may differ depending on an account's region or device.
"We've vetted every method, and the data you provide to us and our vendors is only ever used to determine your age group, so you can pick whichever option you're most comfortable with," Vishnevskiy says.
It's worth mentioning that Discord wasn't subject to a mere controversy online. The age verification rollout comes amidst several lawsuits against the company. Last year, the
New Jersey attorney general
alleged the company misled consumers about child safety features, while
a family sued
both Discord and Roblox, alleging a sex offender communicated with their son on said platforms. Throughout 2026,
Florida opened an investigation
alleging child predators are using the platform to target children, and the
Arkansas attorney general
alleged both Discord and Roblox are knowingly putting children at risk while prioritizing profits over safety. These are just some of
many ongoing
lawsuits.

"We've chosen to launch our stronger protections for teens everywhere using the most privacy-preserving approach we could build, including where it isn't yet required by law, because we believe it's the right thing to do," Vishnevskiy says on a personal note at the end of the announcement.
"By launching a global approach with non-biometric options, we're getting ahead of laws that might ask us to implement something less privacy-focused. The decisions policymakers make now will shape how platforms advance both teen safety and privacy for years to come, and I encourage people to make their perspectives heard where they live."
